data.body:
Read **Who Lives Here? — Comparing Habitats** with a partner or use read-aloud. Explore **Key Words**, then play Matching and Memory. Use **Keep the Ideas Clear** as a reference. Try **Sort and Explain**, **Explain Your Thinking**, and **Check Your Understanding**. Use **Remember the Ideas** to build a memory cue. Read **Questions to Explore**, then complete **Try It with Evidence**.

Explain an answer using a detail from the lesson. Pictures support the activity text. These examples do not show every living thing in a habitat.

Picture panels: Habitats meet needs; Count kinds of living things; Ways to investigate; Look again and compare. Pictures illustrate possible observations. A still picture cannot establish what was heard, elapsed search time, or an unseen animal.

history.title: Who Lives Here? — Comparing Habitats
history.data:
## Who Lives Here?

Look at a pond. Then look at a dry patch of land. Would you expect to find all the same living things?

A **habitat** is a place where a living thing gets what it needs. A pond can be a habitat. So can a tree, a field, or a garden.

A **plant** needs water, light, air, and room to grow. An **animal** needs food, water, air, and a place to live. Their needs help explain where we find them.

A **pond** may have water plants, snails, and fish. A **forest** may have tall trees, birds, and beetles. These are examples, not a list for every pond or forest. Some animals use more than one habitat.

We **observe** by looking and listening with care. We can draw what we find. We do not need to catch or move living things.

To **compare**, look for what is alike and what is different. Count kinds, not just how many things you see. Ten ants of one kind are many animals, but only one kind in your record.

**Diversity** means the variety of living things. A place with more kinds in our record showed more variety during our visit.

One short visit can miss a lot. Some animals hide. Some come out at night. Use the same search time and area for both places. Visit again if you can. Say what you found, and what you still do not know.

questions.question: What is a habitat?
options: A place that meets living needs
A count of leaves on one tree
A drawing of only wild plants
questions.correctAnswer: A place that meets living needs

questions.question: What does diversity describe?
options: The age of one tall tree
The time of one short visit

questions.question: We saw ten ants of one kind. What did we record?
options: No living things in the place

questions.question: What makes our two searches fairer?
options: Use the same time and area
Move plants to the other place
questions.correctAnswer: Use the same time and area

questions.question: What can one short visit tell us?
options: What we noticed on that visit
questions.correctAnswer: What we noticed on that visit

questions.question: Why might two habitats have different living things?
questions.expectedAnswer: Water, light, food, shelter, and other conditions can differ. Different living things need different conditions.

questions.question: Why should we avoid claiming that no animals live in a place?
questions.expectedAnswer: Animals may hide, move through later, or be active at another time. A short search can miss them.

data.question: Can one animal use two habitats?
data.answer: Yes. A bird may feed by a pond and nest in a tree.

data.question: Is a garden a habitat?
data.answer: Yes. Living things can meet their needs there. People can shape habitats too.

data.question: Should we pick up the animals?
data.answer: Observe without moving them. Ask your teacher about safe ways to look.

data.question: Does more animals mean more kinds?
data.answer: No. A large group may all be one kind. Record both counts when you can.
